rationale: The six-card castle-defense subset has current source-backed author PASS decisions for all 36 fields after narrow equivalent wording corrections. Four military-role cards remain open, so the larger ten-card batch remains HOLD. Human source and editorial decisions are recorded; no scripted substantive verdicts were used.

cards.editorialAnalysis: Easy is plausible for a basic fortification feature. The ditch is distinct from a bridge that crosses it; tower, battlement and gate examples are clear alternatives. Notes add facts about their own terms. No duplicate relation with drawbridge.

fields.claimAnalysis: English Heritage defines a moat as a deep, broad ditch around a castle or other site.

proofs.passage: A moat is a deep, broad ditch, which can either dry or filled with water. They can surround a castle, fortification, building or town, providing it with a first line of defence – if attackers got close enough.

cards.editorialAnalysis: Medium is plausible for a specific castle-plan term; no telemetry recalibration is claimed. Mound-plus-enclosure differs from layered concentric walls, entrance towers, and approach defenses. Castle Acre is presented as an example, not universal proof.

proofs.sourceClass: official institutional source; complete source-reader extraction
proofs.title: 1.5 The Middle Ages, Pre-1500 Military Sites: Introductions to Heritage Assets
proofs.captureMethod: Opened official institutional source and preserved the complete returned reader response; passage transcribed verbatim with locator.
proofs.passage: First is the motte-and-bailey, in which the castle was divided into a raised artificial mound (the motte), usually topped by a tower, and an enclosed flat area (the bailey) containing domestic buildings, stables and so forth.

fields.claimAnalysis: Cadw describes concentric castle walls and their relative height.

proofs.passage: The concentric castle had more than one line of defence: an outer wall with additional towers surrounded the inner stronghold. The inner wall was higher, to allow archers to shoot arrows over the heads of soldiers stationed on the outer wall. Sometimes, moats were added to make the castle even stronger.

fields.claimAnalysis: Cadw says a gatehouse protected the entrance and could be a tower or twin towers.

proofs.sourceClass: official institutional source; complete source-reader extraction
proofs.title: Castles of Wales | Cadw
proofs.captureMethod: Opened official institutional source and preserved the complete returned reader response; passage transcribed verbatim with locator.
proofs.passage:
To protect the entrance (often the weakest point of the castle) the gatehouse was built. At first it was a tower with a simple archway in the curtain wall. Later on twin towers, usually D-shaped, were built on each side of the entrance. They usually projected forward to guard the gate and had arrowloops.
Sometimes these towers were made deeper so that there was a passageway through the gatehouse. In this would be gates, portcullises and murder holes.
